questions.problem:
Determine if $v=[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ 4 & -2\end{aligned}].$
If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?
questions.worked_solution:
The eigenvectors are non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ 4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-8+4\text{i} \\ 8\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8{\text{i}}^{2}+4\text{i} \\ 8\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =4\text{i}[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =4\text{i}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=4\text{i}v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =4\text{i}.$

questions.problem:
Determine whether $v=[\begin{aligned}-4+7\text{i} \\ 13\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ 13 & 4\end{aligned}].$
If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?
questions.worked_solution:
The eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ 13 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-4+7\text{i} \\ 13\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-49-28\text{i} \\ 91\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}49{\text{i}}^{2}-28\text{i} \\ 91\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =7\text{i}[\begin{aligned}-4+7\text{i} \\ 13\end{aligned}] \\  & =7\text{i}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=7\text{i}v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =7\text{i}.$

questions.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2-3\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =2-3\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2-3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 2-3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\text{i} & 3 \\ -3 & 3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}3\text{i}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0 \\ -3{x}_{1}+3\text{i}{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(2-3\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=\text{i}{x}_{2}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{i}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{\text{i}}{1}=\text{i}.$

questions.problem:
Given that ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}],$
what is the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 8 \\ -2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-(-2)(8) & =0 \\ 1-2\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +17 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{2\pm \sqrt{(-2)^{2}-4(1)(17)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{2\pm \sqrt{-64}}{2} \\  & =\frac{2\pm 8\text{i}}{2} \\  & =1\pm 4\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =1\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=1+4\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1+4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 1+4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4\text{i} & 8 \\ -2 & -4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}-4\text{i}{x}_{1}+8{x}_{2}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}-4\text{i}{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(1+4\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}\text{i}{x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ \frac{1}{2}\text{i}{x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=2,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ \text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=1-4\text{i}$, we simply compute the complex conjugate of ${\overset{―}{v}}_{1},$ and get

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}} & =\frac{(2)(2)}{(\text{i})(-\text{i})}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}],$
what is the value of $\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}7-\lambda  & 4 \\ -5 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (7-\lambda )(3-\lambda )-(4)(-5) & =0 \\ 21-7\lambda -3\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+20 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +41 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{-(-10)\pm \sqrt{(-10)^{2}-4(1)(41)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{-(-10)\pm \sqrt{-64}}{2} \\  & =\frac{10\pm 8\text{i}}{2} \\  & =5\pm 4\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =5\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5+4\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5+4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 5+4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-4\text{i} & 4 \\ -5 & -2-4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(2-4\text{i}){x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}+(-2-4\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(5+4\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}(-2-4\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}(-2-4\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2+4\text{i} \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=5-4\text{i}$, we simply compute the complex conjugate of ${\overset{―}{v}}_{1},$ and get

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2-4\text{i} \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-5)(-5)}{(2+4\text{i})(2-4\text{i})}=\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
